section.title: First-order linear equations
section.p: Separable equations can be solved by pulling all y’s to one side and all x’s to the other. Many useful equations do not separate.
A tank may have salt entering and salt leaving. A bank account may earn interest while money is also being deposited. A cooling object may sit in a room whose temperature is changing.
These models have a common form:
That is the shape of a first-order linear equation.

subsection.title: Standard form
subsection.p: A first-order differential equation is linear if the unknown function and its derivative appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together.

exercise.title: What makes a first-order equation linear?

statement.p: The standard form is y'+p(t)y=q(t). In your own words, what does the word linear refer to here, and why can p(t) and q(t) still be complicated functions of t without destroying linearity?

hint.p: Linear means linear in the unknown y and its derivative y'. The coefficients are allowed to depend on the independent variable.

subsection.p: The method is not a trick. It is the product rule used backward.

exercise.title: Why does an integrating factor turn the left side into a product rule?

statement.p: Multiplying by \mu=e^{\int p(t)\,dt} converts y'+p(t)y into (\mu y)'. In your own words, why is that not a trick, and what single sentence explains why the method works?

hint.p: The factor is chosen so that \mu'=\mu p(t). Then \mu y'+\mu' y is exactly the derivative of the product \mu y.

subsection.title: Mixing and finance examples
subsection.p: Linear equations appear whenever there is a current amount and an outside input.

exercise.title: What story does the nonhomogeneous term q(t) tell?

statement.p: Mixing tanks and continuous deposits produce linear equations with an outside input. In your own words, why does the solution combine an initial amount with accumulated weighted input, and what would q(t)=0 mean in those stories?

hint.p: After the product rule is restored, integration accumulates the forced term. A zero input is the homogeneous case: the amount then only decays or grows from its starting value.

warning.title: Coefficient warning
warning.p: A solution of a differential equation lives on an interval where the equation makes sense. Singular coefficients split the real line into separate problems.

paragraphs.p: First-order equations already show several personalities. Some are separable. Some are linear. Some are best understood by a phase line. Some require numerical methods.
But many laws of motion do not stop at the first derivative. A spring, a pendulum in a small-angle approximation, and a vibrating string involve acceleration. Their laws begin with
That is the next door: differential equations where the unknown function is governed by its second derivative.

exercise.title: Why can a singular coefficient split one equation into separate problems?

statement.p: The equation y'+(1/t)y=1 is linear, but 1/t is undefined at t=0. In your own words, why must a solution live on an interval where the equation makes sense, and why can a formula such as y=t/2+C/t not be continued through zero?

hint.p: Continuous coefficients are part of the hypotheses. A singularity of p(t) or q(t) is a wall between intervals, not a point to be crossed casually.
